strengths: The Low-Loss Path Finding (LLPF) algorithms are a genuinely novel empirical tool: unlike prior mode-connectivity work (Garipov et al., Draxler et al.) that constructs paths between a single pair of minima, LLPF can build paths toward the origin (Algorithm 2) and across many independently trained models, enabling a broader exploration of the low-loss region.

The empirical validation is relatively thorough for the main results: paths are repeated 200, 40, and 10 times for LeNet5/MNIST, ResNet18/CIFAR10, and CCT7/CIFAR10, with mean and variance reported, and the hyperparameter settings, preprocessing, and compute budgets are documented in detail (Tables 1-5), which supports reproducibility of the experiments.

The variance-sphere abstraction (Equations 2-6), with the approximation Mean(theta)≈0 and the ||OP||² ∝ Var relation, is a simple but useful geometric device, and the paper validates the underlying assumptions empirically (Appendix A.1-A.2) rather than only asserting them.

The post-training generalization result is practically interesting: applying Algorithm 2 to the pretrained torchvision ResNet18 on ImageNet1k improves accuracy from 69.758% to 70.55% without data or hyperparameter changes, suggesting the variance-reduction direction is underexploited by current tuning.
The paper is honest about several failure modes (sharp minima, VGG16 counterexample, test loss not guaranteed low along paths, Adam-trained ResNet18 failing), which is appreciated.
weaknesses: The central claim—that the low-loss space is 'fully connected'—significantly overreaches the evidence. Successfully constructing paths between a finite sample of independently trained minima shows connectivity of the sampled points under the authors' procedure, not that the entire sublevel set S_{L<=thres} is a single connected component. No argument is given for why a failure to connect some pair (e.g., minima separated by permutation symmetries, which the paper does not discuss despite directly relevant literature on permutation symmetry and linear mode connectivity) cannot occur. The claim should be substantially weakened or restructured as an empirical observation.

The 'no redundant parameters' claim (Section 5, Contribution 3) is not convincingly established. The SVD analysis finds the spanned subspace dimension equals min(number of paths, parameter dimension)—which is close to a tautology, since the rank of n vectors cannot exceed n, and paths generated by gradient-descent steps span only the subspace visited by the algorithm, not the geometry of the sublevel set. Moreover, the argument is internally inconsistent: the authors' own variance-sphere construction places layer parameters on a sphere (dimension d_lx - 1), contradicting the claim that the low-loss space has the same dimensionality as the full parameter space. A smooth sublevel set of a scalar loss is generically D-dimensional, so the claim needs much more careful formulation.

The algorithm is fragile and heavily hyperparameter-dependent: for ResNet18 and CCT7 it requires a multi-phase, manually specified layer ordering (Tables 1 and 6), fails on VGG16, fails on Adam-trained sharp minima, and different model-dataset pairs need different configurations. Appendix A.4 experiments (ResNet18@CIFAR100, MobileNet, ShuffleNet) are each run only once. This fragility undercuts the generality of the conclusions and the practical value of the method.

The comparison with AutoNEB is not controlled: the headline result in Appendix A.7 compares a ResNet18 path with L_thres=0.006 against AutoNEB's reported loss of 0.016 for ResNet20 on CIFAR10—a different architecture, and seemingly a different training regime—so 'lower maximum loss than AutoNEB' is not a like-for-like quantitative comparison.

The generalization experiment on ImageNet lacks baselines and uncertainty quantification: no comparison against simple alternatives (e.g., additional fine-tuning epochs, weight-decay-adjusted fine-tuning) and no repetition across seeds, so the improvement of ~0.8% is difficult to attribute specifically to the proposed mechanism.

Connectivity results are threshold-dependent and only two thresholds (0.04, 0.006) are examined for ResNet18; the relationship between the claimed global geometric structure and the chosen L_thres is not analyzed.

Presentation issues: Section 3.1 spends considerable space re-deriving standard training notation; there are typos and informal sources cited (a LessWrong post) as support for SLT claims; and Figures 2/3 rely on smoothed curves whose underlying validity criteria (convergence of layer-wise distances below 1e-1) are assessed only qualitatively in the text.

No release of source code is explicitly confirmed in the manuscript (hyperparameters for Figure 8 are only available 'in the source code'), which limits reproducibility of the full experimental suite.

strengths: The central question — the global geometry of the low-loss sublevel set in the full parameter space, rather than between a fixed pair of minima — is well motivated and connects to a genuine line of work on mode connectivity (Garipov et al., Draxler et al./AutoNEB).
The LLPF algorithms are concretely specified, with full hyperparameter tables, dataset preprocessing, and compute budgets provided in the appendix, which supports reproducibility of the experiments.

The experiments include non-trivial repetition counts (200 for LeNet5, 40 for ResNet18, 10 for CCT7) and report mean/std bands, and Appendix A.7 provides a path with lower maximum training loss than reported for AutoNEB, offering some quantitative comparison to prior work.
The appendix honestly documents failure modes (sharp minima from Adam, VGG16 counterexample, single repeats in A.4), which is useful for practitioners attempting to apply the method.
weaknesses: The headline claim is significantly overclaimed relative to the evidence. Constructing low-loss paths between a handful of models on three small architectures (MNIST/CIFAR-10 scale) cannot establish that the low-loss space of R^D is 'fully connected' — a topological statement about an exponentially high-dimensional set. The paper's own definitions ('continuous', 'fully-connected') are informal, and connectivity across variance spheres is only partially shown: in Figure 3 the path never reaches the origin and training loss increases, so even the model-to-origin connectivity claim is incomplete.

The methodological core is circular and weak as evidence of connectivity. LLPF_M2M constructs the path by repeatedly *training* intermediate points (Train step with r iterations) toward the threshold. This is essentially local fine-tuning stitched along a trajectory, not the discovery of an existing low-loss region; success depends on heavy manual tuning — layer-by-layer ordering, phase schedules, per-model step sizes (Tables 1, 6) — so the reported paths may say more about the algorithm's ability to optimize than about the geometry of the low-loss space. The AutoNEB comparison is also not apples-to-apples (ResNet18 vs. ResNet20 in A.7).

The 'no redundant parameters' claim is essentially trivial and contradicts known results. Any generic sublevel set {L <= threshold} with an interior is full-dimensional, so finding that path directions span the full parameter space does not imply 'all parameters actively contribute'. Moreover, the paper ignores permutation/parameter symmetries [34 is cited but not engaged], which are known to induce lower effective dimensionality of functionally distinct low-loss regions. The SVD analysis (dimension = min(#paths, param dim)) cannot certify full dimensionality D with a limited number of paths.

The 'Variance Sphere' framework is underdeveloped and supported only by approximations (Mean(theta) ~ 0, Var vs. L2 proportionality) that are empirically justified for one model-dataset pair (ResNet18/CIFAR-10) and explicitly admitted to fail elsewhere (VGG16), yet the paper's conclusions are stated as general properties of neural networks.

Several sections read as anecdotal rather than rigorous: the PCA visualization claims about high-frequency changes and layer-wise diagnostics are speculative interpretations of two plots; the generalization result on ImageNet1k (69.758% -> 70.55%) is essentially 340 GPU-hours of continued fine-tuning with no comparison to obvious baselines (weight decay increase, extended training, early stopping, LR schedules), so the practical significance of Algorithm 2 is unestablished.

Writing and presentation issues undermine confidence: Section 3.1 spends a page re-deriving standard training notation; theoretical support leans on a LessWrong blog post [20] and an unrelated master's thesis [5] for central claims about singular learning theory; there are multiple typos and grammatical problems (e.g., 'weigt', 'start-of-the-art', 'This paper makes several contributions to foundational neural network theory' is not warranted by the content).

Test loss along Algorithm 1 paths *increases* for ResNet18 (Figure 2), i.e., the constructed paths leave the practically relevant (test-time) low-loss region, which further weakens the interpretation of these paths as charting a meaningfully connected low-loss space rather than training-loss artifacts.

Generality and robustness of the algorithms are unproven: Appendix A.4 experiments are repeated only once per configuration, prerequisites (flat minima, nearby variance spheres) are characterized only empirically, and no code release is clearly stated, limiting the ability of others to verify or build on the method.

strengths: The LLPF algorithm is a concrete, well-documented procedure (with full hyperparameter tables, computation budgets, and prerequisites for failure modes) for constructing low-loss trajectories between independently trained models and toward the origin, which goes beyond pairwise mode connectivity in AutoNEB [8].

The paper is admirably transparent about limitations: it explicitly documents prerequisites (flat minima needed; sharp Adam minima cause failure), acknowledges that test loss is not guaranteed low along Algorithm 1 paths, and validates its heuristic assumptions (Equations 4 and 5) empirically in Appendices A.1/A.2.

The experiments include useful repetition counts (200/40/10 runs with different seeds) and report variance bands, and the supplementary material covers additional architectures (MobileNet, ShuffleNet) and a lower-threshold configuration (Appendix A.7).

The connection between distance-to-origin trajectories and generalization (Figure 5, including the ImageNet1k experiment on pretrained weights) is an interesting empirical observation that could motivate follow-up work.
weaknesses: The central claim — that the low-loss space is 'continuous and fully connected' — substantially overreaches the evidence. The algorithms produce a discrete sequence of points, each of which is individually trained down below a loss threshold; loss is never verified on the segments between consecutive points, so 'continuity' in any topological sense is not established. Connectivity is only demonstrated for a handful of (model, dataset) pairs under identical hyperparameters, and the paper's own failure cases (sharp minima, VGG16 without BN) show the property does not hold in general.

There is a circularity concern: because the path is constructed by interleaving interpolation with r training steps that explicitly drive each point below L_thres, finding a 'low-loss path' largely reduces to demonstrating that SGD can be used to move between minima — a weaker and much less novel statement than the paper's framing as a contribution to 'foundational neural network theory'.

The 'no redundant parameters' claim (Section 5) is weakly supported. The SVD analysis reports that the spanned dimensionality equals min(#paths, parameter dimensionality), which is close to trivially true, and the inference from 'full-dimensional span' to 'all parameters actively contribute and no redundancy exists at the low-loss-space level' does not follow; it also sits uneasily with known parameter symmetries, which the paper cites [34] but does not reconcile.

The variance-sphere framework rests on approximations that are only partially validated: Figure 7 shows layer means of order 0.1–0.3, which strains the Mean(θ)≈0 assumption (Eq. 5), and Eq. 4 is verified only for ResNet18. The method also requires extensive manual per-model configuration (layer ordering, multi-phase schedules in Tables 1 and 6), which undermines the generality claims, and Appendix A.4 experiments are single-run.

The comparison with AutoNEB is not apples-to-apples: the lower threshold of 0.006 is achieved on ResNet18 while AutoNEB's reported 0.016 is for ResNet20 (Appendix A.7), and the ImageNet1k gain (69.758% → 70.55%) lacks error bars, statistical significance, and comparison to obvious baselines such as continued low-LR fine-tuning or weight-decay tuning.

Terminology is misused or informal ('continuous' and 'fully connected' are defined operationally but clash with their topological meanings; [9] is cited for standard topology), the related-work coverage of linear mode connectivity and permutation-symmetry work is thin, some supporting references are informal (a LessWrong post [20], a master's thesis [5]), and there are multiple typographical errors (e.g., 'weigt+bias', 'start-of-the-art', 'pre-precessing'). Code release is referenced only indirectly ('refer to the source code'), leaving reproducibility of the tuned configurations uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: whether mode connectivity holds for modern architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, ShuffleNet, DLA, CCT) beyond the dated architectures (VGG/ResNet/DenseNet) studied by prior work. This is a well-motivated empirical question.

The core empirical work is fairly thorough: experiments are repeated at least 10 times with independently trained mode pairs, continuity of the constructed paths is explicitly checked via linear interpolation between consecutive points (Figure 5, Appendix A.7), and the geometry-based approximations (Equations 4-6) are empirically validated in Appendices A.1-A.2.

Reproducibility is treated seriously: full hyperparameter tables (Tables 2-4), data preprocessing details (Table 5), and even compute costs are provided (Table 6), and the authors state code will be released.
The limitation that the method does not preserve generalization (test loss/accuracy) along the path is discussed honestly (Section 6), and the failure mode of sharp minima is disclosed.
The idea of connecting modes on different variance spheres (via the M2O + M2M concatenation in Figure 4) is a novel and interesting extension beyond the standard 'identical hyperparameters' setting.
weaknesses: The central comparative claim — that prior methods (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO) fail or are inconsistent on modern architectures — is never substantiated by running any baseline. Table 1 compares worst-case training losses copied from different papers on different models and datasets, and the authors themselves footnote that these numbers 'are not strictly comparable.' The headline contributions (broader applicability, consistency, different-variance-sphere support) are thus largely self-referential.

The 'different training hyperparameters' contribution is supported by only one mechanism (varying weight decay) on three model/dataset combinations (DLA/ResNet18/CCT7 on CIFAR-10); this is narrow evidence for a headline claim.

The method appears fragile and highly hand-tuned. Success reportedly hinges on the layer selection and ordering ('only the layer selection and order determine success'), with orders 'determined manually' for models not using FDF, and prerequisites (nearby variance spheres, flat minima) that are not formally characterized. This casts doubt on easy adoption for new architectures, which is the paper's selling point.

All experiments are on MNIST and CIFAR-10/100. Claims of applicability to 'modern' architectures would be more convincing with at least one larger-scale setting (e.g., ImageNet or a larger transformer), especially given the noted compute costs.

The lack of generalization guarantees (test loss rising along ResNet18 paths despite low training loss) substantially limits the practical value relative to AutoNEB/FGE, which reportedly preserve test performance; the paper's contribution is then mainly a training-loss-landscape artifact.

The method is purely heuristic; there is no analysis or theory explaining why the proposed Move/VarianceCorrection/AngleConformal steps yield connected paths, and the 'variance sphere' formalism (Section 2) adds notational overhead without predictive power.

Several figures show high variance and non-monotonic behavior (e.g., DLA training-loss spikes to ~0.04 in Figure 9), and the quality metric (worst-case training loss) is achieved only after 'targeted hyperparameter tuning and additional compute' (Figure 6), suggesting the reported numbers are best-case rather than typical.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('Algorihtm', 'heigt', 'pre-precessing'), dense and somewhat informal Section 2, and Figure 11's caption claims extensions 'for ResNet18@CIFAR10 and DLA@CIFAR10' while the panels show ResNet18 and CCT7.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap: existing mode connectivity methods (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO) were developed on older architectures, and extending the empirical study to modern architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT) is a useful contribution to the empirical literature.

The experimental coverage is broad: many architectures across MNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100, with repetitions across independently trained mode pairs, and an honest limitations section acknowledging that test loss is not guaranteed along the discovered paths.
Reproducibility effort is substantial: full hyperparameter tables (Tables 2-5), model modification details (A.9), compute cost reporting (Table 6), and supplementary code are provided.
weaknesses: The central comparative claim is not empirically supported by the authors: Table 1 asserts prior methods are 'inconsistent' and LLPF is 'consistent,' but the authors never run AutoNEB, FGE, or SPRO on the modern architectures to show they actually fail. The claim that prior methods do not extend to these architectures is asserted, not demonstrated.

A critical baseline is missing: permutation-matching methods (Git Re-Basin, Entezari et al.) followed by simple linear interpolation are the standard approach for connecting independently trained models. The paper explicitly excludes permutation from scope (Section 3) without testing whether permutation + linear interpolation already succeeds on these architectures, which would trivially undermine the need for the proposed machinery.

The method's success hinges on heavy manual engineering that undermines its generality: layer selection and ordering must be hand-crafted per architecture (the 'FDF strategy'), DLA requires 21 manually specified phases, and the authors themselves state 'only the layer selection and order determine success.' This makes the method closer to a per-architecture recipe than a general algorithm, and no evidence is given that the FDF ordering principles transfer to unseen architectures.

The theoretical framing is weak and heuristic. The 'variance sphere' construction rests on the approximation Mean(theta_lx) ≈ 0 (Eq. 5), yet the paper's own Figure 8 shows layer means as large as 0.1-0.3, and all geometric claims are only 'approximate.' The AngleConformal and VarianceCorrection steps lack any analysis of when or why they work.

The constructed paths do not preserve generalization: Figure 2 shows test loss increasing along the ResNet18 path, and the authors concede (Section 6) that LLPF is confined to training-defined low-loss regions. This substantially limits the practical value relative to prior methods whose paths retained test performance.

The headline 'worst-case training loss' of 0.006 in Table 1 comes from a separately hyperparameter-tuned run (Figure 6), whereas the main results show a maximum around 0.04 — a favorable and somewhat misleading presentation of the method's typical behavior.

Costs are very high and value of components is unclear: connecting two modes takes 21-45 GPU-hours (Table 6), and the purpose of the model-to-origin algorithm (Algorithm 2) — a path from a trained model to a non-low-loss point — is never motivated by any downstream application.

Novelty is incremental: layer-wise mode connectivity is already established (Adilova et al., 2024; Zhou et al., 2023), and LLPF largely combines it with SGD refinement and ad-hoc variance rescaling, without new insight into why connectivity exists.

strengths: Extends mode connectivity to a genuinely broader set of modern architectures (MobileNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, ShuffleNet, DLA, CCT), which prior work (AutoNEB, FGE, SPRO) has not demonstrated; this addresses a real open question about whether mode connectivity persists in newer models.

Strong reproducibility emphasis: experiments repeated across many independently trained mode pairs (>=10 per setting), with error bands reported, and an explicit continuity check via linear interpolation between consecutive path points (Figure 5, Appendix A.7).
New setting of connecting modes trained with different hyperparameters (different 'variance spheres'), supported by a two-stage m2o+m2m procedure and additional results in Appendix A.6.

Unusually thorough reproducibility apparatus: complete hyperparameter tables (Tables 2-5), compute budgets (Table 6), empirical validation of the key approximations (Appendices A.1, A.2), and a stated commitment to releasing code.

Honest limitations section that correctly identifies the main weakness: paths are confined to training-defined low-loss regions and do not guarantee test-metric preservation along the path (e.g., the ResNet18 test-loss increase in Figure 2).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty over layer-wise linear mode connectivity (Adilova et al., 2024). The core recipe—move toward the destination, project back to a per-layer 'variance sphere,' retrain briefly—is a heuristic composition of existing ideas (layer-wise connectivity, variance preservation) rather than a new principle; the 'variance sphere' formalism and Equation 6 are close to trivial, and Equation 4 is only an empirical approximation.

No controlled baseline comparison. Table 1 compares LLPF against AutoNEB/FGE/SPRO using numbers copied from other papers with different models and settings (acknowledged as 'not strictly comparable'), and prior methods are not re-run on the modern architectures. The central claims of broader applicability and better consistency therefore lack an apples-to-apples evidential basis.

Heavy per-architecture engineering undermines generality: success depends critically on hand-designed layer orderings and multi-phase schedules (e.g., 21 phases for DLA in Table 2), and the FDF ordering strategy is justified only empirically. It is unclear how the method transfers to unseen architectures without substantial manual tuning.

Evaluation confined to MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and small-to-medium models; no larger-scale setting (e.g., ImageNet) to substantiate the claim of applicability to 'modern and structurally diverse models.'

Paths do not preserve test performance in several cases (test loss rises along the ResNet18 path), which substantially limits the practical significance relative to prior methods whose paths maintain both train and test metrics; the paper concedes this only in the limitations section.

Algorithmic presentation has ambiguities: the ad hoc step-size formula in Move (Line 14 of Algorithm 1, including an unclear arc-length term |⌢P0D|), inconsistent indexing (loop 'i = 0 to T' but return 'P0...Pn'), and references to a non-existent 'Figure 1 (right)' structure; the AngleConformal learning-rate scaling in Algorithm 2 is unmotivated beyond a heuristic remark.

Significance of Algorithm 2 (model-to-origin) on its own is unclear—the origin is not a useful model—so its value rests entirely on its role as a stepping stone for the different-hyperparameter case, which is demonstrated on only a handful of settings.

Compute cost is substantial (21-45 GPU-hours per path in Table 6) with unclear scaling, which weakens the case for LLPF as a practical tool relative to simpler connectivity procedures where they work.

strengths: Genuinely broad empirical validation: the paper demonstrates mode connectivity between truly independently trained modes across a wide range of modern architectures (MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, CCT) beyond the narrow CNN/ResNet scope of prior work, on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-10.

The reproducibility claim (consistent paths across mode pairs, hundreds of repetitions with ≥10 repeats per setting for main experiments) is unusual for this literature and is supported by variance bands in Figures 2–3 and by a careful consistency check on the baseline's failure modes.

The diagnosis of prior methods is careful and evidence-based: Appendix C documents via cosine-similarity analysis that the released FGE script produces nearly-identical seeds (i.e., not independently trained modes), and Table 9 shows AutoNEB's high variance across runs with the authors' own configurations—this is a valuable correction to the record.

Ablations (Appendix I, Figure 15) are well designed: removing the layer-wise move, the Train step, or the variance correction each degrades the result in a distinct, interpretable way, supporting the claim that each component matters.

The continuity check (Figure 5) and the variance-sphere-range analysis (Appendix K, Figure 20) address plausible objections to the method (discreteness of the path; whether m2o can reach distant variance spheres) with direct experiments.
Hyperparameter configurations, training recipes, preprocessing, and compute budgets are reported in detail (Tables 4–9), and code is stated to be available, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The method's generality claim is undercut by heavy, architecture-specific manual configuration. Success hinges on 'the choice and order of layers,' determined by a hand-crafted Follow Data Flow strategy plus per-architecture phase schedules (Table 4 lists 21 hand-tuned phases for DLA alone), and the paper concedes RegNet endpoint modes violate Equation 4. It is unclear how a practitioner would apply LLPF to a new architecture without repeating this laborious tuning.

The headline comparison in Table 1 is not apples-to-apples: LLPF's worst-case loss (0.006, ResNet18) is compared against AutoNEB on ResNet20 and FGE on ResNet158 with different compute budgets (Table 9: 6.5h vs 21h on H100). The LLPF runtime (21–45 hours per connection, equivalent to thousands of training epochs) is substantial and this cost is not positioned against the baselines in Table 1.

Test-set behavior is weak: the paper acknowledges Algorithm 1 does not guarantee low test loss (ResNet18 test loss rises along the path, Figure 2), and several appendix runs show test loss/accuracy degrading. Since the destination mode's generalization is not preserved, the practical value of the paths is limited—mostly as an empirical probe of the loss landscape rather than a usable tool (e.g., for ensembling or merging).

The theoretical grounding is thin. The 'variance sphere' framing rests on an approximation (Mean(θ)≈0) that the authors admit is violated for some layers (Figure 8 shows DLA deviations up to 0.01, and normalization layers must be excluded), and Equation 4 (Var(θ)≈Var(θ′)) is asserted empirically rather than derived; the path-connectedness conjecture in Section 6 is explicitly unsupported by any framework.

Several key appendix experiments are run only once (Figure 10 notes 'All other experiments are conducted only once' for CIFAR100/ImageNet10), which weakens the reproducibility claims for those settings; the claim of 'hundreds of simulations' is not fully traceable in the text.

Significance is modest: layer-wise linear mode connectivity (Adilova et al., 2024) and the vanishing-variance effect (Tian et al., 2024) are established ideas, and LLPF is an empirical search procedure combining them. No downstream application (model merging, ensembling, distillation, etc.) is demonstrated, and the paper does not extract actionable insight beyond the conjecture in Section 6.

Baseline coverage is narrow: only FGE and AutoNEB are compared. Benton et al. (2021) SPRO and other connectivity methods are cited but not evaluated, and no comparison on identical architecture/compute is provided for the main Table 1 numbers.

strengths: The empirical scope is unusually broad for mode connectivity work: the method is evaluated on ResNet18, DLA, CCT7, MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, VGG, DenseNet, and LeNet across MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet10, which directly addresses the paper's stated gap that prior evaluations were restricted to dated architectures.

The authors take the claim of 'independently trained modes' seriously and provide convincing forensic evidence (Appendix C) that the FGE training script fixes the seed by default, so the modes used in Garipov et al. (2018) are highly correlated rather than independent. This is a valuable, verifiable finding for the community, supported by per-layer cosine similarity measurements (Tables 2-3).

The paper reports substantial implementation detail: full hyperparameter tables (Tables 4-6), preprocessing pipelines, computational cost (Table 8), and ablations of the layer-wise move, retraining, and variance-correction components (Figures 15-16), which support reproducibility.

The observation that averaging uncorrelated networks reduces parameter variance, and the variance-correction step that counters it, is a sensible and empirically supported design choice, with an ablation showing its removal raises path loss from ~0.04 to ~0.2.
weaknesses: The method is substantially hand-engineered, which undermines the claimed generality and reproducibility. The authors themselves state that 'only the layer selection and order determine success,' and the FDF strategy is presented as an empirical heuristic rather than a principled, automatable procedure. The per-architecture phase schedules (e.g., 21 hand-specified phases for DLA in Table 4) mean that applying LLPF to a new architecture requires significant manual tuning by the authors, so the claim that prior methods are 'inconsistent while ours is consistent' is partly an artifact of manual labor invested in LLPF versus baselines run with authors' default configurations.

The central comparison is weak and confounded. Table 1 compares LLPF on ResNet18 against AutoNEB on ResNet20, and Table 9 compares AutoNEB at 1.9-6.5 hours on an H100 against LLPF at 21 hours on an H100. The claimed advantage in worst-case path loss is thus confounded by both a different architecture and a 3-11x compute budget. There is also no comparison against permutation-based approaches (e.g., Git Re-Basin), which is a notable omission given that such methods are the standard modern approach for connecting independently trained models, and the paper dismisses them via a scope restriction ('without further permutation') rather than empirically.

The theoretical framing is thin and largely decorative. Equations 3-6 constitute elementary algebra relating distance-from-origin to variance under a zero-mean approximation; the 'Variance Sphere' formalism does not yield predictive power or explain why layer-wise connectivity succeeds. The continuity of the path rests on a loose analogy to Neyshabur et al. (2018) plus a single empirical check on CCT7, and Algorithm 1 has no convergence analysis—it iteratively moves toward D with no guarantee of reaching it, and the paper never characterizes when it fails.

Key results undercut the practical significance. Test loss/accuracy along constructed paths is not maintained (ResNet18 case in Figure 2, where test loss rises despite low training loss), meaning the 'low-loss region' guarantee holds only for the training distribution. All experiments are on CIFAR/MNIST-scale models; the ImageNet10 subset is a 10-class variant, not a meaningful test of scale. Additionally, the compute cost (21-45 GPU-hours per connection, equivalent to thousands of training epochs) makes the tool impractical for the envisioned use of 'systematically navigating the low-loss region.'

The novelty is modest. The core mechanism—layer-wise linear connectivity—is explicitly adopted from Adilova et al. (2024) and Zhou et al. (2023); the contribution reduces to an empirical search procedure layered on top of it. The 'different variance sphere' extension (Algorithm 2) is a single experiment (DLA on CIFAR-10, plus two appendix cases) constructed to connect modes differing only in weight decay and learning rate, which is a narrow instantiation of the 'different training hyperparameters' claim.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: the terminology section builds elaborate machinery (modes, low-loss space, variance spheres, angle conformity) that adds little insight; notation switches between P and theta with footnotes; Figure 17's caption says AutoNEB 'could connect Ma and Mc' while the surrounding text says it fails, and Table 9's LLPF row (0.04) is inconsistent with the ~0.05 quoted in the text on the same page, suggesting insufficient care in the final manuscript.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: prior mode-connectivity methods (FGE, AutoNEB) have been validated mainly on dated architectures and do not reliably connect truly independently trained modes. Extending the empirical study to MobileNet, ShuffleNet, EfficientNet, RegNet, DLA, and CCT is a useful contribution.

The reproducibility claim is supported by substantial experimental effort: each main experiment is repeated at least 10 times with different seed pairs, with mean/std curves reported (Figures 2-3), which is more rigorous than much prior work in this area.

The supporting analyses are unusually thorough: Appendix A/B empirically validate the variance-sphere assumptions (Eq. 4-5) across up to 100 independently trained models; Appendix C carefully documents a fixed-seed bug in the original FGE script with cosine-similarity evidence (Table 2); Appendix I provides ablations showing each algorithmic component (layer-wise move, retraining, variance correction) is necessary; Appendices K/L explore the supported variance range and sharp minima.

The cross-hyperparameter connection setting (modes on different variance spheres, Figure 4/13, Appendix G) is new relative to prior mode-connectivity evaluations, and the two-stage m2o+m2m construction is a sensible design.

The paper is honest about scope (Section 3 explicitly excludes permutation/spawning settings) and about limitations of the method, e.g., that test loss is not guaranteed to stay low (Figure 2, ResNet18) and that reverse-direction m2o fails due to exploding gradients.
weaknesses: The algorithm is highly heuristic and hyperparameter-intensive. Table 4 shows up to 21 hand-specified phases per architecture with per-phase layer subsets and step sizes, and the paper states that 'only the layer selection and order determine success.' The proposed FDF ordering strategy is purely empirical and its generality across unseen architectures is not demonstrated; this substantially weakens the claim of a broadly usable, reproducible tool, since applying LLPF to a new architecture likely requires significant manual tuning.

The computational cost is very high (Table 8: 21-45 hours on H100/RTX 5090 per connection, equivalent to thousands of training epochs), which limits practical utility and is not prominently discussed as a trade-off against AutoNEB's 2-6.5 hour runtime. The direct AutoNEB comparison (Table 9) is also on a different, smaller architecture (ResNet20 vs ResNet18), making the head-to-head 'LLPF attains lower worst-case loss' claim in Table 1 somewhat unfair.

Several headline claims rest on single-run evidence. Many appendix experiments (most architectures in Figures 9-12) are 'conducted only once,' and the 'consistent' label in Table 1 covers only a subset of the nine architectures. The claim of supporting 'a broader range of networks' is therefore only partially substantiated.

There is no formal or even semi-formal understanding of why LLPF works; the paper acknowledges (Section 6) that no theoretical framework supports the path-connectedness conjecture. The variance-sphere framework (Eq. 2-6) is a convenient geometric narrative more than an explanatory theory, and the 'sphere' terminology is loose (sets of equal per-layer variance are not spheres in any metric relevant to the loss).

Presentation issues: the source-code URL in the abstract is incomplete ('available in'), which harms reproducibility; terminology such as 'mode' is defined loosely ('any trained parameter that attains low training loss'), making some statements ambiguous; and some empirical assertions (e.g., Eq. 4) are approximate relationships with unquantified tolerance.

Evaluation is restricted to small CIFAR/MNIST/ImageNet10-scale settings; it remains unknown whether LLPF scales to ImageNet-scale models, which is where questions about loss-landscape geometry are most contested.
